A bank credit alert from a personal mobile number. Real banks send alerts from registered sender names, never from 10-digit numbers.
A bank debit alert from a personal mobile number. Real banks never send alerts from 10-digit numbers.
A mobile number is pretending to be a bank.
A money alert from a sender that isn\'t a known bank or one of your contacts.
The sender name only looks like a bank\'s. Real bank alerts come from registered senders like XX-HDFCBK-S.
The sender name mixes letters or digits from different alphabets. Real senders never do this; imitations do.
The sender isn\'t one of the bank\'s registered senders.
The sender name is missing the registered prefix real bank alerts carry.
A credit alert sent as an advertisement. Banks send alerts as transactional messages.
The bank named in the message isn\'t the company that sent it.
The account number doesn\'t match any of your accounts at this bank.
You don\'t seem to have an account at this bank.
It asks you to return money \"sent by mistake\". This is a common scam.
It includes a mobile number to call or pay. Banks never ask this.
It gives a UPI ID or payment link to send the money back to.
It contains a link. Banks don\'t send links in credit alerts.
It asks for your UPI PIN to receive money. A PIN is only ever needed to pay, never to receive.
Approving a \"request\" to receive money actually sends money from your account.
It arrived soon after a suspicious credit alert, asking about the same money.
It asks you to return a recent credit. Ask the sender to contact their bank instead; never send it back yourself.
